title: Credit Building After Divorce
subtitle: Separate access, responsibility and reporting before rebuilding alone

blocks.text: The relationship can end on Friday. The joint line of credit may stay extremely committed.

This course helps you map every account. Keep four things apart: who can use an account, who is legally responsible, what the lender’s contract says and what your family-law arrangement says. Then protect your payments, contact each institution, check both reports and build a file of your own. Family law varies. This course helps you organize questions and evidence. It does not replace a lawyer or a safety professional.
A separation agreement can assign responsibility between former partners. It does not remove a name from a lender contract on its own. The lender has to approve that change.

items.text: An order or agreement may share out responsibility, but the lender contract stays in place until there is a release, refinance, sale, payout or other approved change.

blocks.text: You can protect both credit files while lenders and lawyers finish the paperwork.
blocks.detail: You will list every account by its role, not from memory, so a signed agreement never leaves a missed payment behind.

blocks.text: FCAC says co-borrowers are equally responsible for a joint card balance. An authorized user is not responsible for repayment, and that use does not build the user’s own history.

items.title: If your safety is at risk, use a safe device and channel. Get qualified support before you confront anyone or change shared arrangements.
Download statements and both reports. List every mortgage, loan, card, line, overdraft, utility, guarantee and pre-authorized payment.
For each one, write the legal names, who has access, the balance, the payment date, the institution, a contact record and the decision needed.
Keep required payments current while legal and lender-approved changes are worked out. A missed joint payment can hurt more than one file.
Secure your own email, phone and banking passwords. Do not move, close or drain joint assets until you understand the contract, the law and the safety risks.

blocks.text: A joint bank account gives each holder access under its rules. All holders may be responsible for transactions and for overdraft debt.

items.title: SOLE BORROWER
items.text: Who may owe: the named borrower. Who may transact: the named borrower and permitted users. First action: secure access and keep required payments current.

items.title: CO-BORROWER
items.text: Who may owe: each borrower may be fully responsible. Who may transact: as the agreement says. First action: request statements and ask the lender about approved options.

items.title: AUTHORIZED USER
items.text: Who may owe: the primary cardholder. Who may transact: the user, until removed. First action: remove access through the issuer and replace the card if needed.

items.title: JOINT BANK ACCOUNT
items.text: Who may owe: all holders may share overdraft debt. Who may transact: each holder, under the account rules. First action: review transactions, overdraft and bank restrictions.

items.title: “Removing a card from my wallet removes my responsibility.”
items.text: Having a card in your wallet and being responsible for the debt are different things. A co-borrower or guarantor stays responsible until the creditor confirms the change in writing.

sections.title: Melanie and the Account That Missed the Memo

paragraphs: Melanie Roy and Daniel Chen have separated after twelve years in Halifax. Their draft agreement says Daniel will pay the joint line and Melanie will cover childcare. They believe the credit question is solved.
The lender was not at those family meetings. It still sees two borrowers on one contract.
In month one, a payment is missed. Each expected the other to cover it, and both get a late notice. Daniel is also still an extra user on Melanie’s card.

Melanie could argue it out by text. She builds an inventory instead: statements, both credit reports and every joint and individual account. She calls each institution and writes down references and next steps.
With legal advice, they set up interim payments until the creditors confirm changes. The card user is removed and the card number is replaced.
Then comes the twist. The line lender will not release either borrower, so they keep it current until the property settlement can pay it out.
Months later, the joint line is paid and closed in writing, and Melanie has an individual account that reports.
Every account has an owner, a payment, a document and a review date. The account that missed the memo finally got it.

blocks.text: Melanie kept five things apart: access, contract responsibility, family-law allocation, payment status and credit reporting.
The inventory showed every role and due date. Interim payments protected both files while the lenders and lawyers finished the formal changes.
You can finish a separation with a credit file that is yours alone.
blocks.detail: You will move through five steps in order, so a shared account never decides your next loan.
blocks.extra: Next, the plan walks you from safety to rebuilding.

items.title: SAFETY AND ACCESS
items.text: If economic abuse, coercion or identity misuse may be happening, safety comes first. Get legal advice and use secure, private communication.

items.title: PAYMENT CONTINUITY
items.text: Keep required payments current when you can, and contact creditors early. Record who paid, when, and from which account.

items.title: LENDER-APPROVED SEPARATION
items.text: Ask what it takes to release a name, refinance, assume, pay out, sell or close. Get the final change and balance in writing.

items.title: BUREAU VERIFICATION
items.text: Review Equifax and TransUnion after changes. Dispute wrong ownership, balances or history, and accounts you do not know.

items.title: INDEPENDENT REBUILDING
items.text: Use your own budget, an emergency reserve and, if you need one, one affordable account that reports. Avoid urgent high-cost replacement debt.

blocks.text: A financial institution’s right of offset may let it use your deposits to cover an overdue debt at that institution. It may apply to some joint accounts. Read your agreements and ask.

items.title: “Closing every older account immediately is always best for my score.”
items.text: Safety or access may require closing an account. But closing an older individual account can cut your available credit or history. Decide account by account, and put safety and legal duties first.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: Why can a separation agreement fail to remove the lender’s claim?
items.detail: It shares out responsibility between former partners. The creditor has to approve any change to its own lending contract.

items.title: Who is generally responsible for an authorized user’s purchases?
items.detail: The primary cardholder. FCAC says the authorized user is not responsible for the balance.

items.title: What should happen to required joint payments while changes are pending?
items.detail: Keep them current when you can, on a written interim schedule, until the lender confirms the formal changes.

items.title: Why look at your deposits and debts at one institution together?
items.detail: A right-of-offset clause may let the institution use deposits to cover an overdue debt, including in some joint-account cases.

items.title: What comes first when economic abuse or coercive control may be present?
items.detail: Your personal safety, private support and qualified legal or community help. Not confrontation, and not score tuning.

blocks.text: Checking both reports can show old joint balances, inquiries you do not know or wrong addresses before the next lender sees them.

Use partial references and store this securely. Leave out passwords, PINs, full account numbers, SINs and anything that could put you at risk.
A complete plan gives every account four anchors: who is responsible, who has access, how payments are protected and a written confirmation of the next change.
Separate the contract, the access, the payments and the reporting, account by account.
blocks.detail: Protect your safety and required payments first. Get lender-approved changes in writing, check both credit files and rebuild on your own once the shared debts are under control.

items.title: Co-borrower
items.text: A person who signed a credit agreement and is responsible for the borrowed balance.

items.title: Authorized user
items.text: A person allowed to use the primary cardholder’s account without being a co-borrower.

items.title: Joint account
items.text: A deposit account shared by two or more holders under the institution’s account rules.

items.title: Guarantor
items.text: A person who promises to repay a debt if the borrower does not, as the agreement says.

items.title: Right of offset
items.text: A contract right that lets a financial institution use deposits to cover an overdue debt. It applies only in some situations.

items.title: Economic abuse
items.text: Using money or resources to control, exploit or harm another person.
